food.text: In the mid-second millennium BCE, the Terramare culture developed in the Po Valley. Its people were agriculturists, cultivating beans, the vine, wheat and flax.
The Terramare culture takes its name from terra marna, the black earth residue of its settlement mounds. This residue has long served the fertilizing needs of local farmers.

The people of the Apennine culture were, at least in part, cattle herdsmen. They grazed their animals over the meadows and groves of mountainous central Italy, including the Capitoline Hill at Rome, as their pottery in the earliest layers of occupation shows.
The Terramare people were still hunters, but they had domesticated animals as well as growing crops. They were also fairly skillful metallurgists, casting bronze in moulds of stone and clay.

Coppa Nevigata was a well-defended and somewhat sizeable coastal site. Its people practiced a variety of subsistence strategies alongside advanced industries such as dye production, so herding was not their only way of living.

When Apennine herdsmen traveled between summer pastures, they built temporary camps or lived in caves and rock shelters. Their culture lived in small hamlets in defensible places, but their range was not confined to the hills.

art.text: Some of the earliest statue menhirs, which frequently depict weapons, were erected by the populations of northern Italy and Sardinia. This sculptural tradition may have come from the steppe, linked to the Yamna culture. It lasted in some regions well into the Bronze Age.

From the Late Neolithic, Aosta Valley, Piedmont, Liguria, Tuscany and Sardinia took part in the pan-Western European Megalithic phenomenon. Later, in the Bronze Age, megalithic structures were also built in Latium, Puglia and Sicily.

The Nuragic civilization of Sardinia began in the early Bronze Age, in the 18th century BC. It grew out of earlier megalithic cultures that built dolmens, menhirs, more than 2,400 Domus de Janas and the imposing altar of Monte d'Accoddi.

Around the end of the third millennium BCE, Sicily imported cultural aspects of the Atlantic world from Sardinia. These included small dolmen-shaped structures, a building type that reached all over the Mediterranean basin.

The Castellieri culture of Istria takes its name from its fortified boroughs, called castellieri. It developed in the Early and Middle Bronze Age, later spread into Friuli and Dalmatia, and lasted from the 15th century BC until the Roman conquest.

Roca Vecchia, on the Adriatic coast of Apulia, has yielded a large wooden 'temple' building from the 2nd millennium BC. The site also has a very large stone fortification wall and the largest set of Mycenaean pottery ever recovered west of mainland Greece.

Coppa Nevigata was a well-defended and fairly large coastal site of the Apennine culture. Alongside a variety of subsistence strategies, its people practiced advanced industries such as dye production.

war.text: At Toppo Daguzzo, a two-tier grave from the Apennine Bronze Age shows growing elite groups. The lower level held eleven burials with valuable pieces, including six males buried with bronze weapons, four females with beads, and a child.

The Canegrate culture of northern Italy, from the 13th century BC, left a necropolis of 165 tombs excavated between 1953 and 1956. These were cremation burials: the urns often held the ashes of several people, and the bronze collars, pins and rings placed with them were warped by the heat of the funeral fire. About 30% of the graves received the ashes of adolescents or children, and the finds suggest a harsh life, a decidedly short average life and a decidedly high rate of infant deaths. Few weapons were found: in the entire necropolis only four swords.

The upper level of the Toppo Daguzzo grave held nearly 10 fractured skeletons with no grave objects at all. Below them lay burials accompanied by valuable pieces, including bronze weapons. The contrast is taken as evidence of hierarchy among social groups.

The tradition of carving weapon-bearing statue menhirs in northern Italy and Sardinia is described as possibly having steppe origins. The Yamna culture is named as the possible source of this sculptural tradition.

science.text: Villages of the Palma Campania culture were buried under volcanic ash after an eruption of Mount Vesuvius that took place around or after 2000 BCE. The culture had taken shape at the end of the third millennium BCE and represents the Early Bronze Age of Campania.

Even after 1200 BC, metal trade kept flowing across the Mediterranean. Studies show that trade in tin neither stopped nor decreased, and lead from Sardinia was still being imported to the southern Levant during the early Iron Age.

Roca Vecchia, on the Adriatic coast of Apulia, has produced some of the best-preserved monumental architecture of the Bronze Age in Southern Italy. It includes a very large stone fortification wall and a large wooden 'temple' building. A team of the University of Salento has explored it since the end of the 1980s.

Apennine pottery is a burnished ware incised with spirals, meanders and geometrical zones. It has been found on Ischia with LHII and LHIII pottery and on Lipari with LHIIIA pottery. These associations date it to the Late Bronze Age as defined in Greece and the Aegean.

The Palma Campania culture is named for the locality of Palma Campania, where the first findings were made. It took shape at the end of the third millennium BCE, before an eruption of Mount Vesuvius buried many of its villages under ash.

Roca Vecchia in southern Italy has yielded the largest set of Mycenaean pottery ever recovered west of mainland Greece. The site is a few kilometres from the modern town of Melendugno and close to the city of Lecce.

politics.text: In the Recent Bronze Age, known as the Sub-Apennine period in Central Italy, communities relocated their sites to defended locations. At this time a settlement hierarchy became clearly visible in places such as Latium and Tuscany.

On Sardinia, with ramifications in southern Corsica, the Nuragic civilization lasted from the early Bronze Age (18th century BC) until the second century AD, when the island was already Romanized. It evolved during the Bonnanaro period from earlier megalithic cultures.

Rome grew out of the gradual union of several hilltop villages during the Final Bronze Age or early Iron Age. The area of Rome was being settled by around 1600 BC, and some evidence on the Capitoline Hill possibly dates as early as c. 1700 BC.

The Apennine culture lived in small hamlets in defensible places in mountainous central Italy. Its pottery appears in the earliest layers of occupation on the Capitoline Hill at Rome, and its people were at least partly cattle herdsmen.

philosophy.text: Nobody knows for certain what the nuraghes of Sardinia were for. They may have been rulers' residences, military strongholds, meeting halls, religious temples, ordinary dwellings, or a mix of these. More than 7,000 of them have been found.

The Nuragic civilization of Sardinia evolved from older megalithic cultures that built dolmens, menhirs and more than 2,400 Domus de Janas. Those cultures also raised the imposing altar of Monte d'Accoddi. Sacred stone building on the island therefore has deep roots.

The Nuragic people of Sardinia buried their dead in collective megalithic tombs that locals call giants' graves. About 800 have been discovered across the island. A stone cairn covers the burial chambers, and some have a cup-shaped entrance like the court cairn tombs of Ireland.

The Bonnanaro culture of Sardinia, the last evolution of the Beaker culture there, lasted from about 1800 to 1600 BC. New peoples from the mainland arrived on the island, bringing new religious philosophies, technologies and ways of life that made the earlier ones obsolete or reinterpreted them. One archaeological reading of their plain, undecorated pottery and their stone and metal weapons (copper and bronze) is that the newcomers were warlike and brought a conflictual thrust to life on the island, and that the old pre-Nuragic world's ideologies seem to have fallen.

Around 1500 BCE, according to Lluís Plantalamor, foreign people arrived on Menorca, and previous ways of life began to be abandoned. The first clusters of houses and villages appeared, with a clear emphasis on defense, including walls and talayots, along with social hierarchy, communal labor specialization, and a gradual increase in the complexity of rituals and religious beliefs.

At El Argar in southeastern Spain, more than a thousand graves have been found inside the houses themselves. The living and the dead shared the same space in this settlement of around 5000 inhabitants.

Small models of nuraghes have often been excavated at religious sites in Sardinia, such as the "maze" temple at Su Romanzesu near Bitti. This suggests the tower may have served as a national symbol of the Nuragic peoples.
One theory says the word nuraghe may come from the name of the Iberian mythological hero Norax. Another proposes a Proto-Basque origin from *nur, meaning stone, with the plural ending -ak.

culture.text: Around the 13th century BC, the Canegrate culture brought a new funerary practice to the Po plain of northern Italy: cremation. It supplanted the earlier custom of inhumation, or burying the body. The culture is thought to represent a first migratory wave of proto-Celtic people from the northwest Alps.

The Castellieri culture of Istria takes its name from its fortified boroughs, called castellieri. It began in the 15th century BC and later expanded into Friuli and Dalmatia. It lasted for more than a millennium, until the Roman conquest in the third century BC.

The Polada culture, named for a locality near Brescia, spread from eastern Lombardy and Veneto to Emilia and Romagna. It formed in the first half of the 2nd millennium BC, perhaps because new people arrived from Switzerland and Southern Germany.

The Urnfield culture took its name from the custom of cremating the dead on pyres and burying their ashes in urns in fields. The cremated bones were often incompletely collected, and sometimes they were simply shattered before burial. By the end of the 2nd millennium BC this tradition had spread through Italy, where the Canegrate culture shows similarities with the urnfields of central Europe.
The Apennine herdsmen lived in small hamlets located in defensible places. When travelling between summer pastures, they built temporary camps or lived in caves and rock shelters.

The Canegrate culture is named for the township of Canegrate, where some fifty tombs with ceramics and metal objects were found in the 20th century. It settled the western Po valley between Lake Maggiore and Lake Como, an area that had earlier been settled by the Scamozzina culture.
